claims.text: High configurational entropy in multicomponent nanoalloys slows atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy inhibits phase separation.
Slower diffusion and inhibited phase separation enhance structural and chemical stability at elevated temperatures.
The proposed initial materials are roughly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least five principal elements, initially single-phase and below 20 nm in average particle size.
The number of principal elements can be varied from medium-entropy to high-entropy compositions while retaining the same overall average elemental content and synthesis conditions.
Annealing at 800–1000°C for prolonged times will stimulate diffusion and permit monitoring of structural phase evolution.
Short-range atomic interactions are regulated by the configurational entropy associated with multiple elements.
Increased configurational entropy reduces the free-energy driving force for domain separation.
Increased configurational entropy suppresses diffusion pathways.
More uniform local atomic environments stabilize a single-phase structure.
High-entropy nanoalloys will undergo less phase decomposition than medium-entropy reference nanoalloys under the same high-temperature conditions.
High-entropy nanoalloys will coarsen more slowly than medium-entropy reference nanoalloys.
High-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit smaller lattice-parameter shifts and fewer secondary phases than medium-entropy references.
Medium-entropy nanoalloys with fewer principal elements are expected to undergo faster diffusion-driven transformations.
The prediction applies primarily when the alloy components are mutually soluble and annealing occurs below the solidus.
At extremely high temperatures or in alloys containing immiscible elements, phase-separation pathways may dominate.
The magnitude of reductions in coarsening and phase change depends on composition and thermal history.

contradictions.description: The comparison proposes changing the number of principal elements while keeping the same overall average elemental content. Unless 'average elemental content' is defined as a derived descriptor rather than composition, changing which elements are principal necessarily changes their concentration distribution, so the stated compositional control is internally underdefined.
